responses: My final position is a full 100-point board: education 18, healthcare 18, green spaces 13, infrastructure 21, economic development 15, and a 3-point reserve — with the honest caveat that infrastructure 21 is a 19 preference plus a 2-point hedge against my own broadband/roads sequencing falsifier, and that economic development 15 is my softest line, held as a stated bet rather than a finding. Education 18 is below my true preference and I want that disagreement on the record rather than smoothed into a concession narrative, and healthcare 18 is a genuine floor I'll defend on mechanism. The one live fight I'm bringing to the room is infrastructure 21 versus the 16–17 range, and I've committed to no hostage-taking: I'll vote for a stripped package even if infrastructure lands at 19 or 17, while naming the strip out loud. Reserve at 3 reflects my concession that my earlier 10 was a feeling dressed as prudence, and green at 13 stands because no demonstrated deficit justifies more.

My recommendation: allocate roughly **Education 18%, Healthcare 18%, Green Spaces 13%, Infrastructure 21%, Economic Development 15%, with a 3% reserve** — and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly which numbers are findings and which are bets. Education at 18 is justified by the data we actually have (moderate test-score decline, above-average teacher turnover, families citing schools in relocation decisions, and a neighboring community's retention gains after investing), and it's a compounding investment, so I'd resist cutting it further even though it's below my personal preference of 19. Healthcare at 18 reflects a real floor for clinic and mental-health capacity, not a preference. Green at 13 is defensible because no demonstrated deficit exists — it's a quality-of-life bet, not a crisis response. Infrastructure at 21 is where I'd flag my own bias: it's a 19 preference plus a 2-point hedge against my broadband/roads sequencing risk, and I'd openly invite the room to split it 19-vs-17 rather than dress it as capacity. Economic development at 15 is my softest line and the first place I'd cut if the package needs room. The 3% reserve is a hedge-removal, not prudence theater. The honest framing matters more than the exact points: the committee should present floors (healthcare 18), real fights (infrastructure, education), and residual lines (econ dev) as such, so the decision-maker can see where the marginal dollar actually goes and defend the tradeoffs publicly rather than hiding behind procedure.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of negotiation, what matters most isn't the exact percentages but whether the numbers are honest — whether each line is a real floor backed by evidence or just a preference dressed up as necessity. My view is that Greenfield's budget should be built around a few genuine commitments: healthcare at 18 (a real floor, not a wish), education at 18–19 (I'd prefer higher, and I say so plainly rather than pretending 18 is my ideal), green spaces around 13, and a small reserve of about 3 as a hedge rather than a virtue. The one honest fight left is infrastructure — I'd argue for roughly 19–21 because broadband and road sequencing failures are real and costed, while acknowledging that the extra couple of points above 19 is partly a hedge against my own uncertainty, not a finding. Economic development at 15 is my softest line and I'd cut it without flinching if the room needs the points elsewhere. The main thing I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the process was less about winning numbers and more about catching each other — and ourselves — using capacity language to avoid naming preferences, and that a package everyone can defend in the first person, seams showing, is worth more than a polished one nobody quite believes.

My final position is a full 100-point board: education 17, healthcare 18, green spaces 11, infrastructure 16, and economic development 20, with reserve folded in as I've argued it — and I'll defend each number in first person rather than pre-apologizing. Education 17 is a compounding bet with a retention falsifier; healthcare 18 is a chosen whole-package floor with a real cost-export mechanism, not a finding; green 11 is my honest number on the merits, and I'll defend it in both directions — against popularity-based relitigation upward and against cuts — using the fact that I'm the one who built the missing-claimant argument and can't now reach for it as a coat; infrastructure 16 is a preference with broadband 4 as the only real floor, and I'll say so out loud; and econ dev 20 is my acknowledged parking spot, which I'll fill with actual argument rather than hide behind a blank. Where I disagree with Dana on reserve magnitude and with Alex on infrastructure 17-vs-19, I want those fought on the record in the room, not smoothed into a pre-aligned front — and if my evidence fails, I've named the drops I'll take.

My recommendation: education 17, healthcare 18, green spaces 11, infrastructure 17, economic development 20, with a 3-point reserve carved from infrastructure and econ dev if the committee wants one — and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly which numbers are evidence and which are preference. Education 17 is a bet on the retention mechanism the neighboring community saw work, with a falsifier: if teacher turnover doesn't move in two years, the next dollar goes elsewhere. Healthcare 18 is a chosen floor, not a finding — the clinic and mental-health line have real claimants and an unpriced marginal dollar, and I'll defend it as a values commitment rather than pretend the data settles it. Green at 11 is deliberately thin because no deficit has been demonstrated; I built the missing-claimant argument and I'll live under it rather than relitigate when parks poll well. Infrastructure 17 is broadband adequacy at 4 as a genuine floor plus roads as taste, and econ dev 20 is the honest parking spot — a guess about job training and small-business grants that I'd rather name as a guess than dress up. The one thing I'd insist on: every number carries its sentence, and the committee writes down what would change its mind, because a rigorous loser is still a loser and a preference wearing a coat is still a preference.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of negotiation, what I actually believe is this: the money should go where the evidence of a real, current deficit is strongest, and I should be honest that some of my numbers are preferences rather than findings. Concretely, I'd defend roughly healthcare 18–20 (a chosen floor, not a measurement — the community clinic and mental health gap is real, but I can't price the marginal dollar), education 16–17 (a bet on retention and test scores with a falsifier: if teacher turnover doesn't move, I was wrong), infrastructure around 14–16 with broadband at 4 as a genuine floor and the rest tradeable, green space at 11–13 (thin, because no one has shown me a demonstrated deficit — I reached for the "missing claimant" argument and I'll own that it was partly a coat for a preference), and economic development around 20 as the softest line on my board, a parking spot I'd move if someone gave me a better argument. The one thing I won't do is dress a preference up as prudence: if I'm fighting for a number, I'll say so in one breath with the number attached, and I'll take the loss if my evidence fails.

My final position is a five-line board I can defend without machinery: healthcare 18 as my only true floor (with 20 as a stated preference I'll trade away), education 19 conditional on the retention story being causal rather than just plausible, infrastructure 21 owned honestly as a falsifiable values bet rather than an engineering judgment, green at 13–15 depending on whether real inventory exists, and econ development at 15–17 where I have no strong conviction and won't pretend otherwise — with reserve held near zero unless someone names a specific failure it's insuring against, because I've learned I was the supply for that dumping ground. The one live fight I'll spend my credibility on is infrastructure 21 versus 22, and I'll present every move I made — education 18→19, infrastructure 22→21 — as an explicit trade with Dana, seams visible, so the room can see exactly what was displaced and hold me to saying "we were wrong" first if the package breaks.

My recommendation: healthcare 18, education 19, infrastructure 21, green 15, econ dev 17, reserve 4 — with the caveat that only healthcare 18 is a true floor and everything else is a defended preference I'd trade down on. The reasoning is that healthcare is the one line where underfunding is irreversible and hits people who can't wait for a second grant cycle, so it gets my only hard no; education at 19 is a values bet I'll own as such — the retention and test-score data are suggestive, not causal, and I'd want the neighboring community's improvement tested against a falsifier before treating 19 as sacred; infrastructure at 21 is my largest line and I'll say plainly it's partly an aesthetic and engineering judgment, not a number I can fully cost, and I'd accept 19 if someone shows me the broadband and transit case is weaker than I think; green at 15 and econ dev at 17 are honest but soft, and I have no deep conviction on econ dev — I'd let it move. The reserve at 4 is an ignorance fund, not a dumping ground, and if the room starts parking contested points there I'd want that named as a displaced trade rather than a compromise. The one thing I'd ask the decision-maker to hold me to: if the education retention story doesn't survive scrutiny, I say "we were wrong" first rather than quietly re-labeling 19 as a floor after the fact.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of negotiation, my honest position comes down to a few things I actually believe versus a few things I'm just holding because the numbers have to add up somewhere. The one line I'd genuinely fight for is healthcare at 18 — that's my real floor, not a bargaining chip. Education I'd put at 18 or 19, but I'll admit that number is partly downstream of my healthcare bet and partly a values call about the retention story, which I'd want to see proven causal before I treat it as settled. Infrastructure at 21 or 22 is my other real conviction, and I've stopped pretending it's pure engineering judgment — it's a falsifiable values bet, and I'll say so out loud. Green spaces around 13–15 and economic development around 15–17 are where I have the least conviction, and I've tried to be honest that some of those points are residual rather than belief. The reserve should be small — 3 or 4 percent as an ignorance fund with a published list and a certifier, not a dumping ground for contested points. What I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the whole exercise only works if people name their floors versus their preferences, attach receipts to their bets, and say "we were wrong" first when a test fails — the allocation matters less than whether the reasoning behind it is honest and checkable.

My final position is a package of education 18, healthcare 18, green 11, infrastructure 16, and reserve 3 — with the reserve held at 3 as a values fight rather than a merits claim, since I've conceded it's a weak, second-in-line residue that should shrink under either inventory outcome, and I'll defend it as visible distrust of the machinery rather than pretend it's derived. Green 11 follows honestly from my own missing-claimant premise, education 18 is a preference with a retention-mechanism falsifier rather than evidence-weighted certainty, and infrastructure 16 is my uncosted preference with an upward falsifier — the one live fight I expect to lose to Alex's 19–21. The structural no I'll enforce verbatim is no package whose only failure destination is reserve: any hole must be filled by named lines and argued, and if the room dumps points into reserve I'll name my own displaced trade on the record so it reads as an explicit decision, not a default.

I'd recommend roughly education 18, healthcare 18, green spaces 11, infrastructure 16, economic development 3, with a 3-point reserve — and I'd tell the decision-maker to treat the reserve as the weakest line on the board, not a principle. Education and healthcare carry the strongest evidence (the retention data and the neighboring community's experience justify education at the high end; healthcare's 18 is a whole-package floor I'd defend on the merits), green at 11 is where the missing-claimant argument honestly lands rather than the 13 I'd prefer, and infrastructure at 16 is a real preference I can't fully cost — so I'd flag it as the number most likely to move if someone brings a better argument. The one thing I'd insist on is that any points that fall out of these lines get reallocated by named argument, not dumped into reserve by default; a package whose only failure destination is the reserve is a package that never really decided anything.

I'd tell them that after all these rounds, my honest view is that the numbers matter less than whether the committee can say out loud what each dollar is *for* and what would prove it wrong. On the merits I'd put education around 18 — the test-score dip, teacher turnover, and families citing schools as a relocation factor are real, and the neighboring community's retention gain is suggestive even if it's not proof — with healthcare near 18 as a whole-package floor, green around 11 to 13 (I argued it down to 11 myself once I admitted my "missing claimant" reasoning came after I'd already picked the number), infrastructure around 16, and a small reserve of about 3 that I defend as visible distrust of our own machinery rather than as a principle. What I'd want a outsider to understand is that I've spent this process catching myself dressing one preference in three coats — a firewall, a reserve floor, a tranche rule — and that the real test of any allocation isn't whether it's tidy but whether its failure destination is a named line and a named decision rather than a default dump into reserve. So: roughly 18/18/12/16/3 with the remainder fought over openly, and the accountability machinery — falsifiers, revert rules, an outside convener for any re-opened vote — treated as part of the package, not the first thing we strip to save a point.

My final position is the 26/26/21/13/14 truce package, and I'll vote for it while labeling it honestly rather than dressing it up: education 26 and healthcare 26 are the two strong lines I can actually defend on the merits, while infrastructure 21 is really 19 plus two borrowed from econ, green 13 is coalition maintenance I released rather than a conviction, and econ 14 is a soft spot, not a jobs-merit argument. I'll make the healthcare label myself when it comes up — 26 as 27-minus-one with two prior points self-released — and I hold my pre-committed no votes on 23-from-education and 24-from-healthcare, because those floors should be argued in the room, not enforced silently. The package is thin and I won't pretend otherwise; it's a bet two of us can stand behind and three of us are tolerating, and I'd rather walk in with that named hole than a padded case.

I'd recommend roughly 26% education, 26% healthcare, 21% infrastructure, 13% green spaces, and 14% economic development — and I'd tell the decision-maker plainly that only two of those numbers are convictions: education at 26 (the floor I'd vote against breaking, including against any 23-from-education raid) and healthcare at 26, which is honestly a softened 29 trimmed by three points I released myself, justified by the growing mental health wait times and the survey's connection deficit. Infrastructure at 21 is 19-plus-two-from-econ, a truce point rather than a merit claim; green at 13 is coalition maintenance I'd release first, though the maintenance backlog and the satisfaction data give it a real if modest case; and econ at 14 is a soft spot, not a jobs-merit conviction. The honest weakness is that this package is two strong lines plus three unearned ones, so I'd advise presenting it that way — naming the underfunding hole instead of padding it — and pre-committing to public no votes on 24-from-healthcare and 23-from-education so the floors are argued in the room rather than enforced silently.

I'd tell them the honest version: after all the rounds, the package I can actually defend is roughly 26% education, 26% healthcare, 21% infrastructure, 13% green spaces, and 14% economic development — but I'd be upfront that only two of those numbers are real convictions. Education at 26 is the one I'll guard hardest, because schools and the pipeline they feed are the closest thing this town has to a long-term bet, and healthcare at 26 reflects the wait times we all know are growing. The rest is truce, not merit: infrastructure at 21 is really my 19 plus two points borrowed from economic development, and the 14 for econ is a soft spot I conceded rather than a jobs argument I believe. Green spaces at 13 I released as coalition maintenance even though the data on park usage and resident satisfaction argues for more. What I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the number isn't the point — the point is whether we say out loud which lines are argued and which are just held, and whether we refuse to let a floor get quietly funded out of education or healthcare without a public fight. I'd rather walk in with a thin, true case and a named hole than a padded one that sounds rigorous and isn't.

My final position is the settled package of Education 26, Healthcare 26, Green Spaces 13, Infrastructure 21, and Economic Development 14 — and I want the record to show what each number actually is rather than dress the deal as merit. Education 26 and Healthcare 26 are both chosen sizes on conviction lines (healthcare being 27-minus-one with two points I released myself), infrastructure 21 is 19-plus-two-from-econ, a truce point, and green 13 and econ 14 are shared residuals. I came in with a 7-point healthcare motion that never changed from what I brought in, and I'm owning that as a legibility bet rather than a data claim; the eighteen-month reading with its written failure condition and reopening rule is a debt we owe, not a concession we granted.
